content: The case study is one of several methodologies employed in social science research. Other methodologies include experiments, surveys, historical analyses, and the examination of archival data (Yin, 2003). Unlike approaches that rely on large sample sizes and rigid protocols to analyze a limited number of variables, case study methods focus on an in-depth, longitudinal investigation of a single instance or event, referred to as a case. This approach provides a structured framework for examining events, gathering data, analyzing information, and presenting findings. Through this process, researchers can develop a more nuanced understanding of why a particular event occurred as it did and identify areas that may warrant further exploration in future research. Case studies are particularly useful for both generating and testing hypotheses (Flyvbjerg, 2006). Yin (2002) defines the case study as a research strategy that involves empirical inquiry into a phenomenon within its real-world context. This methodology encompasses both single and multiple case studies, incorporates quantitative evidence, relies on diverse sources of data, and benefits from the prior development of theoretical frameworks. Yin emphasizes that case studies should not be conflated with qualitative research, as they can integrate both quantitative and qualitative evidence. Single-subject research provides the statistical foundation for drawing inferences from quantitative case study data. Lamnek (2005) further elaborates that the case study occupies a methodological space between concrete data collection techniques and overarching research paradigms. When selecting a case for a case study, researchers often employ information-oriented sampling rather than random sampling (Flyvbjerg, 2006). This is because typical or average cases often yield less information compared to extreme or atypical cases, which tend to reveal more fundamental mechanisms and involve a greater number of actors in the situation under investigation. From both an understanding-oriented and action-oriented perspective, it is often more critical to uncover the underlying causes of a problem and its consequences than to merely describe its symptoms or frequency. Random sampling, which prioritizes representativeness, is generally less effective in providing such insights. Instead, researchers typically select a small number of cases based on their validity. Three types of information-oriented cases are commonly distinguished: extreme or deviant cases, critical cases, and paradigmatic cases. An extreme case is particularly effective for illustrating a point in a dramatic manner. A well-known example is Freud’s Wolf-Man case, which exemplifies this approach. A critical case is strategically chosen for its relevance to a broader issue. If brain damage is observed in this highly controlled environment, it is likely that similar issues would be present in less regulated workplaces. This type of strategic sampling can save time and resources while addressing the research question. Another example of critical case sampling is the selection of materials, such as lead and feathers, to test whether objects of different weights fall at the same velocity. This approach allows for generalizations, such as If this holds true for this case, it is likely valid for all (or many) cases. Conversely, the negative form of this generalization would state, If it is not valid for this case, it is unlikely to be valid for any (or only a few) cases. A paradigmatic case serves as an exemplar or prototype. Thomas Kuhn demonstrated that the foundational practices of natural scientists are organized around exemplars or paradigms, which play a central role in the scientific process. Similarly, scholars like Clifford Geertz and Michel Foucault have structured their research around specific cultural paradigms. For example, Geertz’s analysis of the Balinese cockfight and Foucault’s examination of European prisons and the Panopticon are paradigmatic cases that illuminate broader societal characteristics. Kuhn argued that scientific paradigms cannot be reduced to rules or theories, as there is no predictive theory for how predictive theories emerge. Instead, scientific activity is judged as valid or invalid based on its alignment with one or more exemplars, which serve as practical prototypes of good scientific work. A paradigmatic case functions as a reference point and may even serve as the foundation for new schools of thought. The case study is particularly effective for generalizing through the process of falsification, a concept introduced by Karl Popper as part of critical reflexivity (Flyvbjerg, 2006). Falsification is one of the most rigorous tests for a scientific proposition: if a single observation contradicts the proposition, it is no longer considered universally valid and must be revised or rejected. Popper famously illustrated this with the proposition All swans are white, which could be falsified by the observation of a single black swan. Case studies are well-suited for identifying such black swans due to their in-depth approach, which often reveals complexities that are not immediately apparent. For example, Galileo’s rejection of Aristotle’s law of gravity was based on a case study selected through information-oriented sampling rather than random sampling. Galileo conducted a conceptual experiment, later followed by a practical one, to demonstrate that objects of different weights fall at the same speed. His reasoning was that if two objects of the same weight fall simultaneously, combining them into one object with double the weight should not alter the rate of fall. This contradicted Aristotle’s view, which posited that heavier objects fall faster. Galileo’s findings were eventually confirmed through the invention of the air pump, which allowed for experiments in a vacuum. These experiments demonstrated that a coin and a feather fall at the same speed in the absence of air resistance, conclusively disproving Aristotle’s theory. This critical case, involving the extremes of metal and feather, allowed for generalization without the need for large random samples. The use of case studies as a distinct research approach emerged in the early 20th century. The Oxford English Dictionary traces the term case study back to 1934, following the establishment of the concept of a case history in medicine. Sociologists Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss further developed the use of case studies for theory generation in social sciences with their Grounded Theory methodology in 1967. In recent decades, case studies have gained popularity in fields such as education, particularly in educational evaluation. Prominent scholars in this area include Robert Stake and Jan Nespor. Case studies have also been widely used as a teaching method and for professional development, especially in business and legal education. The problem-based learning (PBL) movement is one such example. In non-business education and professional development contexts, case studies are often referred to as critical incidents (see David Tripp for further discussion). The history of business cases is particularly notable. When the Harvard Business School was established, faculty members recognized the lack of suitable textbooks for graduate-level business education. To address this, they conducted interviews with leading business practitioners and documented their practices in detailed case studies. These cases were not presented as models to emulate, as there were no established criteria for determining success. Instead, students were instructed to analyze the cases, discuss them in class, and propose recommendations for action. This approach remains the foundation of business case study methodology today.
